Create these URLs on your server. Send each one only to the user who needs it. Do not log them.

## Data

| Topic | Short answer | Details |
| - | - | - |
| How long boat keeps data | While a sandbox runs, and at least 14 days after it stops. Saved snapshots have no scheduled expiry. | [Data retention](/data-retention#how-long-boat-keeps-data) |
| Erase a sandbox | `boat delete <id>`. You cannot undo it. | [Delete](/data-retention/delete) |
| Keep nothing after a stop | Zero data retention | [Zero data retention](/data-retention/zero-data-retention) |
| No snapshots or no logs at all | Snapshots off, monitoring off | [Snapshots and monitoring off](/data-retention/snapshots-and-monitoring-off) |
| Where data is stored | Machines in Germany, Finland and France. Snapshot copies can be stored outside the EU. | [Compliance and uptime](/compliance#data-location) |
| AI keys | Keep real keys out of sandboxes with the AI credentials proxy | [AI credentials](/ai-credentials) |

SOC 2, uptime, data location and security reports are on [Compliance and uptime](/compliance).


# Setup scripts
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/setup

Run commands when a sandbox starts: repository setup scripts, a per-sandbox setup file, or commands from your own code. Includes how to fail when setup fails.

There are three ways to run commands when a sandbox starts. You can use them together.

| | Where you set it | Runs | Best for |
| - | - | - | - |
| [Repository setup script](#repository-setup-scripts) | Dashboard, or the environments API. No CLI command. | At **every** start: create, resume and fork | `npm install`, `git pull`, migrations |
| [`--setup-file`](#per-sandbox-setup-file) | `boat new` or `POST /sandboxes` | **Once**, at create, in the background | A script that differs between sandboxes |
| [Commands from your code](#driving-setup-from-your-code) | Your program | When you call | Setup that must succeed before you continue |

Do not script slow installs. Put them in a [saved snapshot](/snapshots/templates). Then they are already installed when the sandbox starts. Read [Environment, setup script or saved snapshot?](/environments/choose).

## Repository setup scripts

A repository setup script belongs to one repository of an [environment](/environments).

* It runs at every start of the sandbox: create, resume and fork. Make it safe to run many times.
* It runs inside the folder of that repository, in a login `bash` shell.
* boat adds `set -e` at the top. The script stops at the first failed command.
* Your environment variables and secret files are already in place.
* It does not run when the environment is [safe for third parties](/environments/access#safe-for-third-parties), when you use `--no-env`, or when the **GitHub repositories** toggle is off.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
npm ci
npm run db:migrate
```

Mark the script **blocking** if your agent must wait for it:

| Mode | Effect |
| - | - |
| Blocking | boat holds prompts to the [integrated agent](/integrated-agents) until the script finishes. Commands and SSH work at once. |
| Non-blocking | The script runs at the same time as everything else. |

When a script fails, the sandbox writes its output to `/tmp/routine-logs/` inside the sandbox.

### Set a repository setup script

In the dashboard:

1. Open [Dashboard > Environment](https://boat.dev/dashboard?tab=environment).
2. Under GitHub repositories, click **Setup** below the repository.
3. Write the script. Select **Blocking** if your agent must wait for it.
4. Save the environment.

With the API, send the full repository list of the environment. This call **replaces** the list. Include every repository that you want to keep.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
# $BOAT_API_BASE is https://boat.dev/api/v1. Get $ENV_ID and $REPO_ID as in Repositories.
curl -sS -X PUT "$BOAT_API_BASE/environments/$ENV_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"repositories\":[{\"repositoryId\":\"$REPO_ID\",\"baseBranch\":\"main\",\"setupScript\":\"npm ci\\n\",\"setupBlocking\":true}]}"
```

Read [Repositories](/environments/repositories) to get the ids. Running sandboxes keep the old script until you [upgrade](/environments/versions) them.

## Per-sandbox setup file

Use this when the work is different for each sandbox. Pass a local script when you create the sandbox. The limit is 64KB, UTF-8.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat new --setup-file ./setup.sh
```

* The script runs in the background after the sandbox is ready. It never delays `ready`.
* It runs as the user `user`, not as root. Use `sudo` for root commands.
* It runs once. A resume does not run it again. A fork does not copy it.

Watch it with `boat info <id>`:

| Field | Values |
| - | - |
| `setupStatus` | `pending`, `running`, `done`, `failed` |
| `setupError` | Exit code and the end of stderr, when it failed |

## Fail when setup fails

boat does not delete a sandbox when its setup fails. Check the result yourself, then delete the sandbox. This is not the same as [fail fast](/machines/fail-fast), which is about machine availability.

Run the setup with `boat exec`. `boat exec` exits with the exit code of the command.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
set -euo pipefail
id=$(boat new --json | jq -r 'select(.event == "ready") | .id')

if ! boat exec "$id" --cwd web-app --timeout 600 'bash ./setup.sh'; then
  echo "setup failed in $id" >&2
  boat delete "$id" --yes
  exit 1
fi
```

For a setup longer than 600 seconds, run `boat exec <id> --timeout 0 'bash ./setup.sh'`. It waits with no limit and exits with the exit code of the setup.

With `--setup-file`, poll `setupStatus` instead:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
id=$(boat new --setup-file ./setup.sh --json | jq -r 'select(.event == "ready") | .id')
while :; do
  status=$(boat info "$id" --json | jq -r .sandbox.setupStatus)
  case "$status" in
    done) break ;;
    failed) boat info "$id" --json | jq -r .sandbox.setupError >&2; boat delete "$id" --yes; exit 1 ;;
    *) sleep 5 ;;
  esac
done
```

## Driving setup from your code

1. Configure your secrets in the environment.
2. Run the commands that you need.

The script reads normal environment variables. It reads the secret files at their configured paths. No sensitive data goes through the command line.

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
sandbox_id="$(boat new --json | jq -r 'select(.event == "ready") | .id')"
boat exec "$sandbox_id" --cwd my-repo --timeout 300 "bash ./setup.sh"
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/$SANDBOX_ID/commands" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"command":"bash -lc ./setup.sh","cwd":"my-repo","timeoutSeconds":300}'
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
await sandbox.command({
  sandboxId,
  command: "bash -lc './setup.sh'",
  cwd: "my-repo",
  timeoutSeconds: 300,
});
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
from boat_sdk.models.command_request import CommandRequest

sandbox.command(
    sandbox_id,
    CommandRequest(command="bash -lc './setup.sh'", cwd="my-repo", timeout_seconds=300),
)
```

* A command stops after 30 seconds by default. Set `timeoutSeconds` (`--timeout` in the CLI) up to 600.
* For longer work, use `boat exec --timeout 0` or the SDK helper `run_command` / `runCommand`. They have no time limit. Read [Background commands](/long-running-tasks/background-commands).
* Call when the sandbox is `ready`. A call made earlier waits for the start, or gets a retryable `sandbox_starting` error.

To pipe a script that is not on the sandbox yet, use SSH. SSH streams stdin, stdout and stderr. You do not have to copy the script first.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat ssh bx_f7k2q9hd -- bash -s < ./setup.sh
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> On Windows, run this from Node, Python, WSL, Git Bash or `cmd.exe`. Native PowerShell pipelines can keep stdin open for native executables. Then the command hangs.

## Related

* [Environments](/environments)
* [Saved snapshots](/snapshots/templates)
* [Long-running tasks](/long-running-tasks)
* [SSH access](/ssh-access)


# Snapshots
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/snapshots

boat saves the disk of your sandbox all the time. Stop, resume, fork, save a saved snapshot or download your files.

A snapshot is a saved copy of the disk of your sandbox. boat makes snapshots for you. You do not have to do anything.

* boat saves the disk every minute while the sandbox runs.
* boat saves it one more time when the sandbox stops.
* Each save keeps only what changed, so saves are small and fast.

Memory and running programs are not in a snapshot. A resume within 10 minutes of a stop usually gets the same machine back, with memory and programs. After that, a resume is like a reboot. Read [Resume within 10 minutes](/snapshots/stop#resume-within-10-minutes).

## What you can do with a snapshot

| You want | Use | Command |
| - | - | - |
| Stop paying, keep the disk for at least 14 days | [Stop](/snapshots/stop) | `boat stop <id>` |
| Your sandbox back after a stop | [Resume](/snapshots/resume-and-fork#resume) | `boat resume <id>` |
| A second sandbox that copies this one | [Fork](/snapshots/resume-and-fork#fork) | `boat fork <id>` |
| A fixed starting point for many sandboxes | [Saved snapshot](/snapshots/templates) | `boat snapshot <id> <name>`, then `boat new --from <name>` |
| Files from a snapshot on your computer | [Download](/snapshots/download-and-delete) | `boat snapshot pull <snapshotId>` |

Resume and fork always use the newest snapshot. You cannot go back to an older one. To keep a state that you can go back to, save a [saved snapshot](/snapshots/templates). Read [Restore an older snapshot](/snapshots/resume-and-fork#restore-an-older-snapshot-roll-back).

```mermaid theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
%%{init: {"theme": "base", "fontFamily": "IBM Plex Mono", "themeVariables": {"fontFamily": "IBM Plex Mono", "fontSize": "14px", "primaryColor": "#F1F3F9", "primaryBorderColor": "#263FA9", "primaryTextColor": "#060606", "secondaryColor": "#E0E3F2", "tertiaryColor": "#FEFEFE", "lineColor": "#060606", "textColor": "#060606", "mainBkg": "#F1F3F9", "nodeBorder": "#263FA9", "clusterBkg": "#FEFEFE", "clusterBorder": "#C4C4C4", "edgeLabelBackground": "#FEFEFE", "actorBkg": "#F1F3F9", "actorBorder": "#263FA9", "actorTextColor": "#060606", "actorLineColor": "#9E9E9E", "signalColor": "#060606", "signalTextColor": "#060606", "labelBoxBkgColor": "#F1F3F9", "labelBoxBorderColor": "#263FA9", "noteBkgColor": "#E0E3F2", "noteBorderColor": "#E0E3F2", "noteTextColor": "#060606", "sectionBkgColor": "#F1F3F9", "altSectionBkgColor": "#FEFEFE", "taskBkgColor": "#263FA9", "taskBorderColor": "#263FA9", "taskTextColor": "#FEFEFE", "gridColor": "#E0E0E0"}, "flowchart": {"padding": 16, "nodeSpacing": 48, "rankSpacing": 48, "curve": "linear"}, "sequence": {"boxMargin": 16, "actorMargin": 48, "noteMargin": 16, "messageMargin": 32, "mirrorActors": false}, "state": {"padding": 16}, "gantt": {"barHeight": 24, "barGap": 8, "fontSize": 14, "sectionFontSize": 14}}}%%
flowchart LR
  A[Sandbox disk] -->|every minute, and on stop| B[(Newest snapshot)]
  B -->|boat resume| C[Same sandbox, new machine]
  B -->|boat fork| D[New sandbox, copy of the disk]
  B -->|boat snapshot id name| E[Saved snapshot]
  E -->|boat new --from name| F[New sandbox, copy of the saved snapshot]
  B -->|boat snapshot pull| G[Files on your computer]
```

For the words boat uses, and the words other providers use, read [Concepts](/concepts).

## What comes back

* Your files, your installed packages and your system settings come back.
* Your Docker volumes and containers come back. Containers that ran start again.
* Services that you enabled with systemd start again by themselves.
* Programs that you started by hand do not come back. Start them again.
* Memory, open connections and `/tmp` do not come back.
* The IP address changes.

The list above is for a resume on a new machine. A resume within 10 minutes of the stop usually gets the same machine, and everything comes back.

For the full list, read [What a snapshot saves](/snapshots/whats-saved).

## A stop saves first

A stop saves the disk before boat removes the machine. If the save fails, boat keeps the sandbox running and tries again for up to 3 days. After 3 days, boat does a forced stop. Read [When a stop is refused](/snapshots/stop#when-a-stop-is-refused).

Some apps keep recent changes in memory. Chrome is an example. To save these changes before a stop, use a pre-stop command. Read [Stop a sandbox](/snapshots/stop).

## Cost

* Automatic snapshots are free, with no count limit. boat keeps the newest one for **at least 14 days after the stop**. Automated retention cleanup can delete it later once enabled. Read [Keep a stopped sandbox longer than 14 days](/snapshots/stop#keep-a-stopped-sandbox-longer-than-14-days).
* Saved snapshots have no scheduled expiry. Your plan includes some. You cannot save one during the free trial. Each one above that costs \$0.056 a day from the wallet. Unpaid extras can be deleted after 7 days. Read [Saved snapshot pricing](/snapshots/templates#saved-snapshot-pricing).

How long boat keeps each snapshot is in [Data retention](/data-retention#how-long-boat-keeps-data).

## Learn more

> [card] [Stop a sandbox](/snapshots/stop)
>
> What a stop does, how to save app state first, and what happens when a stop is refused.

> [card] [Resume, fork and restore](/snapshots/resume-and-fork)
>
> Get your sandbox back, make a copy, or get older files back.

> [card] [Readiness and resume speed](/readiness)
>
> What works at `ready`, and how to wait for the rest in a script.

> [card] [What a snapshot saves](/snapshots/whats-saved)
>
> Which folders come back, Docker, caches, and how to leave files out.

> [card] [Saved snapshots](/snapshots/templates)
>
> Save a sandbox under a name. Deploy many sandboxes from it. Share it with another account.

> [card] [Download a snapshot](/snapshots/download-and-delete)
>
> Look inside a snapshot and download its files.


# Download a snapshot
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/snapshots/download-and-delete

Look inside a snapshot and download its files, also from a stopped sandbox. Get one file, one folder or the whole home folder.

You can read the files of a snapshot without starting the sandbox. The sandbox can be stopped.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat snapshot pull bx_f7k2q9hd -o ./restore    # newest snapshot of this sandbox
```

## Look inside and download

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat snapshots                                 # across your sandboxes
boat snapshots bx_f7k2q9hd                     # one sandbox
boat snapshot latest bx_f7k2q9hd
boat snapshot tree <snapshotId>                # files + sizes
boat snapshot pull <snapshotId> -o ./restore   # download and reassemble
boat snapshot pull <snapshotId> -o ./restore --path /home/user/project/report   # one folder only
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
curl -sS "$BOAT_API_BASE/snapshots" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY"
curl -sS "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/bx_f7k2q9hd/snapshots/latest" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY"
curl -sS "$BOAT_API_BASE/snapshots/<snapshotId>/tree" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY"

# one file, or a folder as .tar, straight from a snapshot
curl -sS "$BOAT_API_BASE/snapshots/<snapshotId>/files?path=projects/app/.env" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" -o .env
curl -sS "$BOAT_API_BASE/snapshots/<snapshotId>/files?path=projects/app" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" -o app.tar

# a changed system file: use its absolute path
curl -sS "$BOAT_API_BASE/snapshots/<snapshotId>/files?path=/etc/nginx/nginx.conf" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" -o nginx.conf
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
await sandbox.listSnapshots();                                    // across your sandboxes
await sandbox.listSandboxSnapshots({ sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd" }); // one sandbox
await sandbox.getLatestSandboxSnapshot({ sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd" });
await sandbox.getSnapshotTree({ snapshotId: "<snapshotId>" });    // files + sizes

const file = await sandbox.getSnapshotFile({
  snapshotId: "<snapshotId>",
  path: "projects/app/.env",
});
const archive = await sandbox.getSnapshotDownload({ snapshotId: "<snapshotId>" });
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
sandbox.list_snapshots()                          # across your sandboxes
sandbox.list_sandbox_snapshots("bx_f7k2q9hd")     # one sandbox
sandbox.get_latest_sandbox_snapshot("bx_f7k2q9hd")
sandbox.get_snapshot_tree("<snapshotId>")         # files + sizes

file = sandbox.get_snapshot_file("<snapshotId>", path="projects/app/.env")
archive = sandbox.get_snapshot_download("<snapshotId>")
```

`$BOAT_API_BASE` is `https://boat.dev/api/v1`.

## What `pull` downloads

`boat snapshot pull` writes two folders:

| Folder | Holds |
| - | - |
| `home_user/` | Your `/home/user` |
| `docker/` | Your Docker named volumes |

They hold the files exactly as they were at that snapshot.

`--path` extracts only the files under that path. It still downloads the whole snapshot.

`pull` recreates symlinks that stay inside `home_user/` and `docker/`. On every platform it skips a link that points outside that tree, such as `/etc`, or one that resolves through another symlink. On Windows it also skips links unless Developer Mode is on or the shell runs as administrator. It prints how many entries it skipped.

`pull` is for your home folder and your volumes. A snapshot also saves your changes in `/etc`, `/usr`, `/opt`, `/root`, `/srv` and `/var`, other home folders, and folders that you create at `/`. To get one of these files, ask the file endpoint for its absolute path, as in the curl example above.

## Download a saved snapshot

A saved snapshot downloads the same way. Use its snapshot id, not its name.

1. Get the id: `GET $BOAT_API_BASE/saved-snapshots/<name>` returns it in `snapshot.snapshotId`.
2. Download: `boat snapshot pull <snapshotId> -o ./restore`.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
curl -sS "$BOAT_API_BASE/saved-snapshots/web-stack" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY"
```

The SDKs have no `pull`. Use `getSnapshotDownload`, then put the files together on your computer.

You can also see the files, and download them, in the [Snapshots](https://boat.dev/dashboard?tab=snapshots) tab of the dashboard.

For all calls, read the [Snapshots API](/api/reference/snapshots/list-snapshots).

## Which snapshots you can download

The newest snapshot of a sandbox stays while it runs and for at least 14 days after it stops. After that, automated retention cleanup can delete it once enabled ([details](/snapshots/stop#keep-a-stopped-sandbox-longer-than-14-days)). Older snapshots stay in the list only for a short time, usually less than a day. Resume and fork always use the newest one. Read [How long boat keeps data](/data-retention#how-long-boat-keeps-data) and [Restore an older snapshot](/snapshots/resume-and-fork#restore-an-older-snapshot-roll-back).

* After the deletion, the sandbox stays in your list as expired. Resume and fork fail with `409 snapshot_data_expired`.
* To keep the data longer, save a saved snapshot before the deletion: `boat snapshot <id> <name>`. This works on a stopped sandbox. A saved snapshot does not expire.

If you need more time, write to [support](/support).

## Delete a sandbox

A stop keeps the snapshots. A delete erases them for good. To delete a sandbox or one snapshot, read [Delete a sandbox or snapshot](/data-retention/delete).


# Resume, fork and restore
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/snapshots/resume-and-fork

Get a stopped sandbox back, copy a sandbox, and get files from an older snapshot back. Resume and fork always use the newest snapshot.

Resume and fork both start a machine from the **newest** snapshot of a sandbox.

| | Resume | Fork |
| - | - | - |
| You get | The same sandbox, with the same id | A new sandbox, with a new id |
| The source sandbox | Is the sandbox | Keeps running. boat does not change it |
| Use it to | Continue your work after a stop | Try something risky, start a second branch of work, give one sandbox to each of your users |

To deploy many sandboxes from one fixed state, use a [saved snapshot](/snapshots/templates) instead of forks.

## Resume

A resume brings a stopped sandbox back on a new machine. The sandbox keeps its id and its disk.

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat resume bx_f7k2q9hd
boat resume bx_f7k2q9hd --type large      # different size: small, default, large or xlarge
boat resume bx_f7k2q9hd --ttl 7200        # new lifetime, in seconds
boat resume bx_f7k2q9hd --no-auto-stop    # runs until you stop it
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/bx_f7k2q9hd/resume" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type":"large","ttlSeconds":7200}'
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
await sandbox.resume({
  sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd",
  type: "large", ttlSeconds: 7200,
});
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
from boat_sdk.models.resume_request import ResumeRequest

sandbox.resume(sandbox_id="bx_f7k2q9hd", resume_request=ResumeRequest(type="large", ttl_seconds=7200))
```

`$BOAT_API_BASE` is `https://boat.dev/api/v1`.

* Every stop makes the snapshot that a resume needs: `boat stop`, auto-stop, and a stop for an empty wallet. Only `boat stop --force` and [snapshots off](/data-retention/snapshots-and-monitoring-off#snapshots-off) skip it.
* boat keeps the snapshot of a stopped sandbox for at least 14 days. After that, automated retention cleanup can delete it once enabled. Resume and fork fail with `409 snapshot_data_expired` once deletion completes. Save a [saved snapshot](/snapshots/templates) before day 14 to keep the disk longer. Read [Keep a stopped sandbox longer than 14 days](/snapshots/stop#keep-a-stopped-sandbox-longer-than-14-days).
* A sandbox in `error` can also resume. It comes back from its newest snapshot. Read [A sandbox is in error](/troubleshooting#a-sandbox-is-in-error).
* To change the size, stop the sandbox first. Then resume with `--type`. A resume of a running sandbox with a new `--type` fails.
* You can resume on a smaller size. If the sandbox has more data than the smaller size can hold, boat refuses the resume and does not change the sandbox. Read [Machines](/machines).
* If you do not send `ttlSeconds`, the sandbox keeps its current lifetime.
* To turn auto-stop off, send `null` (`--no-auto-stop`).
* `boat resume` waits until the sandbox runs a command. Then it returns. To return at once, add `--no-wait`.
* The IP address changes at every resume.

What works at `ready`, and what comes a few seconds later, is in [Readiness and resume speed](/readiness).

## Fork

A fork copies a sandbox into a new sandbox. The source keeps running, and boat does not change it.

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat fork bx_f7k2q9hd
boat fork bx_f7k2q9hd --type small
boat fork bx_f7k2q9hd --ttl 600         # lifetime for the fork, in seconds
boat fork bx_f7k2q9hd --no-auto-stop    # runs until you stop it
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/bx_f7k2q9hd/fork" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type":"small","ttlSeconds":600}'
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
const forked = await sandbox.fork({
  sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd",
  type: "small", ttlSeconds: 600,
});
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
from boat_sdk.models.fork_request import ForkRequest

forked = sandbox.fork(sandbox_id="bx_f7k2q9hd", fork_request=ForkRequest(type="small", ttl_seconds=600))
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> A fork of a **running** sandbox uses its last background snapshot. boat takes one each minute. Writes from the last minute or so can be missing from the fork.
>
> For an exact copy, save a saved snapshot first: `boat snapshot <id> <name>`. A save of a running sandbox takes a new snapshot at that moment. Then run `boat new --from <name>`. A fork of a **stopped** sandbox has everything, because the stop took the last snapshot.

What the fork gets from the source:

* The whole disk, as it was at the newest snapshot.
* The per-sandbox variables of the source. If you send your own `env`, the fork uses yours.
* The exact environment version of the source. Read [Environments](/environments).

What the fork does not get:

* The lifetime of the source. A fork stops after 1 hour by default, even if the source has auto-stop turned off. To change this, send `ttlSeconds` or use `--no-auto-stop`.
* A per-sandbox setup script (`--setup-file`) of the source. That script runs one time, on the sandbox that you created with it.

To make many copies at once, read [Make many copies](/snapshots/templates#make-many-copies).

## Restore an older snapshot (roll back)

Resume and fork always use the newest snapshot. **You cannot resume or fork an older snapshot.** There is no point-in-time restore.

The snapshot list of a sandbox holds only recent snapshots. boat removes older ones, usually within a day. Read [How long boat keeps data](/data-retention#how-long-boat-keeps-data).

To get files back from an older snapshot that is still in the list:

1. Find the snapshot: `boat snapshots <sandboxId>`.
2. Download its files: `boat snapshot pull <snapshotId> -o ./old`. Or download one path. Read [Download a snapshot](/snapshots/download-and-delete).
3. Copy the files into the sandbox: `boat scp`.

To keep states that you can go back to, save a saved snapshot at each point. A saved snapshot has no scheduled expiry, but unpaid extras can be deleted. For example, save one each day from cron:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat snapshot bx_f7k2q9hd "daily-$(date +%F)"
```

Then start a sandbox from any of them with `boat new --from daily-2026-10-12`. Your plan includes some saved snapshots at no cost. Read [Saved snapshot pricing](/snapshots/templates#saved-snapshot-pricing).

## How fast a sandbox comes back

A resume, a fork or a deploy is ready in a few seconds, whatever the size of the disk. boat downloads your files in the background. What works at `ready`, how to wait for the rest, and how to make the first start faster are in [Readiness and resume speed](/readiness).

## No machine free

A resume or a fork waits for a machine when none is free. To get an answer at once instead, read [Fail fast when no machine is free](/machines/fail-fast).


# Stop a sandbox
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/snapshots/stop

What a stop does, how to wait for it in a script, how to save app state first, and what happens when a stop is refused.

A stop saves the disk, then removes the machine. A stopped sandbox costs nothing. Run `boat resume` to get it back.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat stop bx_f7k2q9hd
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> **boat keeps the disk of a stopped sandbox for at least 14 days.** After that, an automated retention job can delete it when enabled. The job currently reports candidates without deleting them in production. Once deleted, the sandbox cannot resume or fork. Save a saved snapshot before day 14 if you need the disk longer. Read [Keep a stopped sandbox longer than 14 days](#keep-a-stopped-sandbox-longer-than-14-days).

* There is no pause. A stop removes the virtual machine and keeps a copy of the disk. A resume starts a new machine with that disk.
* A stop keeps the disk. A resume within 10 minutes usually gets the same machine back, with memory and running programs. Do not count on it. After 10 minutes, memory and running programs are gone. Read [Resume within 10 minutes](#resume-within-10-minutes).
* Every stop saves the disk first: `boat stop`, [auto-stop](/long-running-tasks/auto-stop) and a stop for an empty wallet. Only `boat stop --force` and [snapshots off](/data-retention/snapshots-and-monitoring-off#snapshots-off) skip the save.
* To erase the sandbox for good, delete it. Read [Delete a sandbox](/data-retention/delete).

## State names

The CLI and the dashboard show one set of names. The API and webhooks show another.

| CLI and dashboard | API and webhooks | Meaning |
| - | - | - |
| `stopping` | `archiving` | boat saves the disk and removes the machine |
| `stopped` | `archived` | The disk is saved. The sandbox costs nothing |

The API reports a stopped sandbox as `archived`. The webhook event for a stop is `sandbox.archived`. The field `archiveAfter` is the auto-stop time. These are names only. A stopped sandbox is not moved or deleted.

## Keep a stopped sandbox longer than 14 days

| Day after the stop | What happens |
| - | - |
| 0 to 14 | The disk is kept for free. `boat resume` and `boat fork` work. |
| After 14 | Eligible for automated retention cleanup once enabled. The job currently reports candidates without deleting them in production. Once deleted, resume and fork fail with `409 snapshot_data_expired`. |

* A resume starts the 14 days again from the next stop.
* A [saved snapshot](/snapshots/templates) has no scheduled expiry. Save one from a stopped sandbox before day 14.
* Your plan includes 10 or more saved snapshots. Each one after that costs \$0.056 a day from the wallet. Delete it to stop the charge.

To keep the disk of a sandbox that stays stopped a long time, save a saved snapshot before day 14. Then start from the saved snapshot instead of the sandbox:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat snapshot bx_f7k2q9hd customer-42     # works on a stopped sandbox
boat new --from customer-42               # later: a new sandbox with that disk
boat snapshot rm customer-42              # when you no longer need it
```

To pay the least, save the saved snapshot only for sandboxes that are still stopped on day 13. Sandboxes that resume earlier need no saved snapshot. Record the stop time in your app when you call `boat stop`, and run the save from a daily job.

## Wait for the stop in a script

`boat stop` returns when the stop starts, with state `stopping`. It does not wait for `stopped`.

To wait, poll `boat info` until the state is `stopped`:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat stop "$ID"
until [ "$(boat info "$ID" --json | jq -r .sandbox.state)" = "stopped" ]; do sleep 2; done
```

With the API, poll `GET /sandboxes/{sandboxId}` until `sandbox.state` is `archived`.

A second stop is safe to send:

| Sandbox is | `POST /sandboxes/{sandboxId}/stop` returns |
| - | - |
| Already stopping | `202` with the stop operation that runs |
| Already stopped | `200` with the last stop operation |

You do not need to wait before a plain `boat resume`. A resume during `stopping` takes back the same machine, with no restore. If boat cannot take the machine back, the resume fails with `409 sandbox_stopping`. The answer carries a `Retry-After` header and the stop operation.

### Resume within 10 minutes

boat keeps the machine for 10 minutes after the sandbox reads `stopped`. These 10 minutes are not billed.

* A plain `boat resume` in those 10 minutes usually takes back the same machine, with no restore.
* Memory, running programs, open terminals and the IP address are then still there.
* boat can release the machine early. The resume then starts a new machine from the snapshot, like a reboot.
* After 10 minutes, a resume always starts a new machine from the snapshot.

Make your work survive a new machine: run it as an [always-on service](/long-running-tasks/always-on-services).

Wait for `stopped` before you resume with a new `--type` or `--environment`. Such a resume always starts a new machine.

## What a stop does

boat does these steps in this order:

1. boat runs your [pre-stop command](#save-app-state-before-a-stop), if you have one.
2. boat stops your Docker containers. Each container gets 30 seconds to exit.
3. boat takes the last snapshot of the disk.
4. boat turns off the machine and removes it.

boat does not shut down the operating system. Only Docker containers get a stop signal. Your other programs get no signal.

A program that runs during the stop does not run its cleanup code. Its files go into the snapshot as they are at that moment.

To clean up, use one of these:

* Clean up when the sandbox starts again. An enabled systemd service with an `ExecStartPre=` step runs at every resume. Read [Always-on services](/long-running-tasks/always-on-services#run-an-always-on-service).
* Run your own cleanup first, then run `boat stop`.

## Save app state before a stop

Some apps keep recent changes in memory. They write them to disk later.

Chrome is an example. Chrome writes new cookies to disk every 30 seconds, or when it closes. If you stop the sandbox a few seconds after a login, the snapshot has the old cookies. A kill signal does not help, because Chrome then exits without saving.

To fix this, put a command in the file `~/.boat/pre-stop`. boat runs it at every stop, before the last snapshot.

The example below closes Chrome. It needs Chrome to have a debug port. Start Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=9222`.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
mkdir -p ~/.boat
cat > ~/.boat/pre-stop <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# Ask Chrome to close over its debug port, so it writes its cookies.
node -e '
fetch("http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/version").then(r => r.json()).then(v => {
  const ws = new WebSocket(v.webSocketDebuggerUrl);
  ws.onopen = () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({ id: 1, method: "Browser.close" }));
  ws.onclose = () => process.exit(0);
}).catch(() => process.exit(0));'
# Then wait for it to exit.
for i in $(seq 30); do pgrep -f remote-debugging-port=9222 >/dev/null || exit 0; sleep 1; done
EOF
chmod +x ~/.boat/pre-stop
```

A Chrome that you started without the flag does not answer, so the command does not close it. A Chrome that you opened from the desktop is an example. Start it again with the flag.

How the pre-stop command runs:

* It runs as `user`, in your home folder.
* It has 60 seconds. After that, boat stops it.
* It runs on `boat stop` and on auto-stop.
* It does not run on `boat stop --force`. It does not run when you save a saved snapshot.
* If it fails or takes too long, the stop continues.
* The file is on the disk. Resumes, forks and saved snapshots keep it.

## When a stop is refused

A stop saves the disk first. If the save fails, boat refuses the stop. The sandbox keeps running, so the unsaved work stays on its disk. boat tries again by itself and sends you an email.

**You do not pay while the stop waits.** The billing meter pauses at the first refused stop. Your balance and your invoice both show the pause. You do not need to ask for a refund.

* The meter stays paused while the stop waits, even if you or your scripts use the sandbox.
* The meter starts again when the sandbox stops.
* The meter also starts again when you resume the sandbox, because a resume cancels the stop.
* If the refused stop was an auto-stop, the meter starts again when you use the sandbox again.

The stop waits until a save works. Then the sandbox stops by itself.

If this happens again and again, snapshots fail on that sandbox. The stop error shows the last snapshot error. We get an alert. Also [contact us](/support), so that we look at your sandbox.

> [!WARNING]
>
> The boat agent in the sandbox uploads snapshots to `boat.dev` and to snapshot storage. If you block outbound traffic in the sandbox, let the agent service `ascii-agent.service` out, or every save fails and every stop is refused. An nftables `socket cgroupv2` rule stops to match when the agent restarts, for example on a boat update. Load that rule again each time `ascii-agent.service` starts.

To stop the sandbox now, run `boat stop --force`. In the API, send `{"force": true}` in the body. The reply has `"forced": true` when boat reads the force. The sandbox stops with its last good snapshot. **You lose everything written after that snapshot.**

After 3 days of failed saves, boat does a forced stop by itself. You then lose everything written after the last good snapshot. boat sends you an email one day before it does this.

## Why a sandbox stops by itself

Auto-stop is the most common cause. For every cause and how to check it, read [Why did my sandbox stop?](/troubleshooting#why-did-my-sandbox-stop).

## Stop without saving

To never save a sandbox, turn [snapshots off](/data-retention/snapshots-and-monitoring-off#snapshots-off) for your account or for one sandbox. boat then never saves it, and a stop erases it.


# Saved snapshots
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/snapshots/templates

Save a sandbox under a name, use it as a template for many new sandboxes, make many copies at once, and share it with another account.

A saved snapshot is a copy of a sandbox disk that you save under a name. Each new sandbox that you start from it gets the same disk. Use a saved snapshot as a template: install your tools one time, then start many sandboxes from it.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat snapshot bx_23456789 web-stack     # save the disk under a name
boat new --from web-stack               # start a new sandbox from it
```

## Automatic and saved snapshots

| | Automatic snapshot | Saved snapshot |
| - | - | - |
| Who makes it | boat, every minute and at each stop | You, with `boat snapshot <id> <name>` |
| Belongs to | One sandbox | Your account or your organization |
| Kept | The newest one while the sandbox runs and **at least 14 days after it stops**. Older ones expire ([details](/data-retention#how-long-boat-keeps-data)) | No scheduled expiry, even after the sandbox is gone. Unpaid extras can be deleted ([details](/data-retention#how-long-boat-keeps-data)) |
| Used by | `boat resume`, `boat fork`, `boat snapshot pull` | `boat new --from <name>` |
| Price | Free, no count limit | Included in your plan, then \$0.056 a day each from the wallet ([details](#saved-snapshot-pricing)) |

## Save a saved snapshot

1. Create a sandbox. Install everything: runtimes, packages, your app.
2. Save it with `boat snapshot <id> <name>`. This saves the disk as it is now, under the name.
3. Start each new sandbox with `boat new --from <name>`.

Each deploy is ready in a few seconds. The time and the cost stay about the same, whatever the saved snapshot holds.

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat new                                # install your stack, then:
boat snapshot bx_23456789 web-stack     # save it under a name
boat new --from web-stack               # deploy as many as you want
boat snapshots                          # your saved snapshots, then recent automatic snapshots
boat snapshot rm web-stack              # remove it and release its storage
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/saved-snapshots" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"sandboxId":"bx_23456789","name":"web-stack"}'

curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"from":"web-stack","environment":"users","env":{"TENANT_ID":"acme"}}'
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
await sandbox.saveSavedSnapshot({ sandboxId: "bx_23456789", name: "web-stack" });

// poll until it settles at "ready"
const saved = await sandbox.getSavedSnapshot({ name: "web-stack" });

await sandbox.create({ from: "web-stack", environment: "users", env: { TENANT_ID: "acme" } });

await sandbox.listSavedSnapshots();
await sandbox.deleteSavedSnapshot({ name: "web-stack" });
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
from boat_sdk.models.saved_snapshot_save_request import SavedSnapshotSaveRequest
from boat_sdk.models.create_sandbox_request import CreateSandboxRequest

sandbox.save_saved_snapshot(SavedSnapshotSaveRequest(sandbox_id="bx_23456789", name="web-stack"))

# poll until it settles at "ready"
saved = sandbox.get_saved_snapshot("web-stack")

sandbox.create(create_sandbox_request=CreateSandboxRequest(
    var_from="web-stack",
    environment="users",
    env={"TENANT_ID": "acme"},
))

sandbox.list_saved_snapshots()
sandbox.delete_saved_snapshot("web-stack")
```

`$BOAT_API_BASE` is `https://boat.dev/api/v1`. In Python, `from` is a reserved word, so the field is `var_from`.

* `current` works only in a terminal that has the boat shell integration. In scripts, pass the sandbox id.
* If the sandbox runs, the save takes a new snapshot of its disk. The call returns at once with status `saving`. The capture runs after that, in the background. A file that is on the disk when you run the command is in the save.
* A write after the call can also land in the save. To save an exact state, wait until `getSavedSnapshot` shows `ready` before you write again.
* If the sandbox is stopped, the save uses its last snapshot.
* The save does not run your [pre-stop command](/snapshots/stop#save-app-state-before-a-stop).
* `boat snapshots` shows the size of each saved snapshot.

Docker containers and every tagged Docker image are in a saved snapshot. The build cache is not. Read [Docker](/snapshots/whats-saved#docker).

### A saved snapshot does not depend on its sandbox

A saved snapshot is a full copy. The source sandbox can change, stop or be deleted. The name still deploys the exact disk that you saved.

A saved snapshot does not expire.

## Make many copies

To start many sandboxes with the same disk, save a saved snapshot one time. Then start each sandbox with `--from`. Do not fork a running sandbox again and again: each fork gets a slightly different disk.

Each start counts against your start limits. Above a limit, the start fails with `429 rate_limited`.

| Plan | Starts per minute / hour / day | Sandboxes at once |
| - | - | - |
| \$20 | 12 / 60 / 200 | 100 |
| \$100 | 30 / 210 / 840 | 300 |
| \$500 | 65 / 420 / 1,680 | 1,000 |
| \$2000 | 90 / 600 / 2,400 | 2,000 |
| [Free trial](/free-trial) | 5 / 25 / 75 | 2 |

The example below paces for the \$20 plan. Change the wait for your plan.

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
# 50 copies, paced for 12 starts per minute
for i in $(seq 50); do
  boat new --from web-stack --json > "sandbox-$i.json" &
  sleep 5
done
wait
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
const ids: string[] = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
  const created = await sandbox.create({ from: "web-stack" });
  ids.push(created.sandbox.id);
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5000)); // 12 starts per minute
}
```

* To get an answer at once when no machine is free, add `--fail-fast`. Read [Fail fast when no machine is free](/machines/fail-fast).
* To retry a create safely, send an `Idempotency-Key` header. A retry with the same key returns the same sandbox.
* During the free trial, you can run 2 sandboxes at once. Read [Free trial](/free-trial).

## Update a saved snapshot

Save the same name again:

1. Resume the sandbox, or use any sandbox that has the setup you want.
2. Update your tools.
3. Run `boat snapshot <id> <name>` with the same name.

The name now deploys the new disk. boat removes the old copy. Sandboxes that you already deployed do not change.

If the new save fails, the name keeps the last good save.

To keep the old version too, save under a new name, for example `web-stack-v2`.

## Saved snapshots and environments

A saved snapshot holds the **disk**. An [environment](/environments) holds the **settings**. Most setups use both.

| | Saved snapshot | Environment |
| - | - | - |
| Holds | Installed packages, builds, caches | Repositories to clone, secrets, logins |
| Answers | "What is already on this machine?" | "What can this machine use?" |
| Costs | Storage, and a few seconds per deploy | Nothing |
| To change it | Save the name again. Deployed sandboxes do not change | boat makes a new version. Running sandboxes change only when you upgrade them |
| Used at | Deploy, one time | Every start, resume and fork |

A simple rule: what you put in a Dockerfile goes in a saved snapshot. What you put in a `.env` file goes in an environment. Use both together:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat new --from web-stack --environment users --env TENANT_ID=acme
```

This sandbox starts with your tools installed, none of your logins, and one variable of its own.

> [!WARNING]
>
> A deploy from a saved snapshot does **not** get the **environment** of the source sandbox. It gets the environment from `--environment`, or your default environment. So a saved snapshot that you saved while logged in to your GitHub does not give that access to its deploys.
>
> A deploy **does** get the **per-sandbox variables** of the source, the same as a fork. Each `--env KEY=VALUE` that you gave the source is set on every deploy, unless the deploy sends its own `env`. Do not put a secret in `--env` on a sandbox that you will save as a saved snapshot.

## Saved snapshot pricing

Each account and each organization has included saved snapshots: 10 for every \$20 of plan per seat, and never fewer than 10. A \$100 plan includes 50. You cannot save a snapshot during the free trial. Saved snapshots that you already have stay free. You can keep more. Each saved snapshot above the included count costs \$0.056 a day (\$1.68 for 30 days).

* boat takes this cost each day from your [wallet](/billing#wallet). The plan's included VM time does not pay it.
* When you remove a saved snapshot, it stops costing from the next day.
* A save goes to your active organization, or to the one that you pass with `--org`. All members of an organization share its included saved snapshots. See [Team images](#team-images-saved-snapshots-of-an-organization).
* If a member leaves an organization, the organization keeps the saved snapshots that the member saved for it.
* To save a new saved snapshot above the included count, the wallet needs money. With an empty wallet, the save fails with `credit_required`.
* With [zero data retention](/data-retention/zero-data-retention) on, you cannot save a saved snapshot.

`boat snapshots` shows how many saved snapshots you keep and their monthly cost. The API gives the same numbers in `allowance` on `GET /saved-snapshots`.

### When your wallet is empty

1. Your sandboxes get the usual grace period. Read [Why did my sandbox stop?](/troubleshooting#why-did-my-sandbox-stop).
2. Your saved snapshots above the included count get 7 days.
3. boat sends you an email. It lists these saved snapshots and the date that boat deletes them. boat sends a reminder one day before.
4. If your wallet is still empty on that date, boat deletes them.

boat never deletes your most recent saved snapshots, up to the included count.

To cancel the deletion, add money to the wallet: `boat wallet pay 20`. You can also remove saved snapshots until you are at or below the included count.

## Team images: saved snapshots of an organization

A saved snapshot that you save under an organization belongs to the organization. Every member sees it in `boat snapshots` and starts sandboxes from it. No share code is necessary.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat --org acme snapshot bx_23456789 web-stack   # save it for the organization
boat --org acme new --from web-stack             # any member deploys it
```

* The name counts on the organization's allowance, not on yours.
* Any member can save the name again to update it.
* The member who saved it, or an owner or admin of the organization, can remove it or make a share code.
* It holds the disk of the member who saved it. If that member turns on zero data retention or deletes their account, boat deletes it. If the member only leaves the organization, the organization keeps it.
* A sandbox that a teammate deploys gets none of your logins. Before it opens, boat removes your Claude, Codex and GitHub logins, your SSH keys and your environment secret files from its disk. The teammate's own environment then applies. Files that you cloned yourself stay.
* Saved snapshots that you saved before 2026-10-22 under `--org` stay personal. Save them again under `--org` to make them team images.

## Share a saved snapshot with another account

A share code lets another boat account deploy one of your saved snapshots. The other account runs `boat new --from <code>`. The new sandbox is in their account, and they pay for it.

A share has two values:

| Value | Prefix | Use |
| - | - | - |
| Share code | `bsh_...` | The secret that you give out. The other account deploys with it |
| Share id | `shr_...` | Not secret. You use it to revoke the code |

1. Create the source sandbox.
2. Install your tools and save them: `boat snapshot <id> <name>`.
3. Make a code: `boat snapshot share <name>`. Give the `bsh_...` code to the other account.

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat snapshot share web-stack              # prints the bsh_... code one time only
boat snapshot shares web-stack             # list share ids (shr_...), use counts, status
boat snapshot unshare web-stack shr_...    # revoke one code, by its share id

# in the other account
boat new --from bsh_...
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/saved-snapshots/web-stack/shares" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY"

curl -sS "$BOAT_API_BASE/saved-snapshots/web-stack/shares" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY"

curl -sS -X DELETE "$BOAT_API_BASE/saved-snapshots/web-stack/shares/shr_..." \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY"

# in the other account
curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"from":"bsh_..."}'
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
const { shareCode, share } = await sandbox.createSnapshotShare({ name: "web-stack" });

await sandbox.listSnapshotShares({ name: "web-stack" });
await sandbox.revokeSnapshotShare({ name: "web-stack", shareId: share.id });

// in the other account
await sandbox.create({ from: shareCode });
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
from boat_sdk.models.create_sandbox_request import CreateSandboxRequest

created = sandbox.create_snapshot_share("web-stack")

sandbox.list_snapshot_shares("web-stack")
sandbox.revoke_snapshot_share("web-stack", created.share.id)

# in the other account
sandbox.create(create_sandbox_request=CreateSandboxRequest(var_from=created.share_code))
```

* boat shows the code one time only, when you make it. boat keeps only a hash of the code.
* If you lose a code, revoke it and make a new one.
* A code has 256 random bits. Nobody can guess it.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Before the other account can use its sandbox, boat removes these from the disk: your logins and API keys, the secret files of your environment, your repository clones, and your SSH authorized keys.
>
> boat shares everything else on the disk. This includes secrets that you wrote into files yourself.

The other account gets:

* A sandbox in their account, which they pay for.
* None of your per-sandbox variables. Their own environment applies, as with any `boat new`. To use no environment, they send `noEnv: true` (`--no-env`).

What happens to a code over time:

| You do this | Result |
| - | - |
| Save the same name again | The code deploys the new save |
| Revoke the code | New deploys with the code fail. Sandboxes made before keep their copy |
| Remove the name | boat removes its codes too. Sandboxes made before keep their copy |
| Delete your account | Sandboxes made from your codes keep their copy |

A wrong or revoked code fails with `404 snapshot_not_found`.

API keys need these scopes:

| Action | Scope |
| - | - |
| Make or revoke a code | `snapshot.write` |
| List codes | `snapshot.read` |
| Deploy from a code | `sandbox.create` and `snapshot.read`, the same as any `from` |


# What a snapshot saves
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/snapshots/whats-saved

Which folders a snapshot saves and which it does not. Docker containers, images and build cache, tool caches, /tmp and the IP address after a resume.

A snapshot saves the parts of the disk that you changed. It does not save the operating system that every machine already has.

## Saved and not saved

> [card] Saved
>
> `/home/user`: your code, files and settings
>
> Every other home folder under `/home`, for example a second Linux user
>
> Folders that you create at `/`, for example `/code` or `/data`
>
> Docker **named volumes** (`/var/lib/docker/volumes`)
>
> Your Docker **containers** and every tagged Docker **image**, used by a container or not ([read more](#docker))
>
> **Your changes** in `/etc`, `/usr`, `/opt`, `/root`, `/srv` and `/var`, with their owners and permissions. This means installed packages, systemd services, system settings, cron tables and the data of databases that you install with apt.

> [card] Not saved
>
> The operating system and the tools that come with every machine
>
> The identity of the machine: hostname, IP address, network settings, [SSH host keys](/ssh-access#verify-the-host-key)
>
> `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`, `/var/cache`, the journal logs (`/var/log/journal`) and Docker internals other than volumes. Put files that must survive a stop in `/home/user` or in a folder that you create at `/`.
>
> Your cache folder `~/.cache`, except Playwright browsers and the Deno cache ([read more](#tool-caches))
>
> Running programs, memory and open ports. A resume within 10 minutes of a stop usually gets them back on the same machine ([read more](/snapshots/stop#resume-within-10-minutes))
>
> The Docker **build cache**, and untagged `<none>` images ([read more](#docker))

The IP address changes at every resume and fork. To reach a port at a fixed address, use a [public URL](/hosting).

### Keep a hostname

A snapshot does not save `/etc/hostname`, so the hostname changes at every resume and fork. To keep a hostname, set it from an enabled systemd service. Enabled services start again after each resume and fork.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/set-hostname.service >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Set a fixed hostname

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/hostnamectl set-hostname my-sandbox

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF
sudo systemctl enable --now set-hostname.service
```

To name a sandbox in boat, set its `name` instead. The hostname is not used for that.

## Deleted files stay deleted

A deletion is a change, so the snapshot saves it too. For example, remove a coding agent that comes with the machine:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
sudo rm -rf /opt/kimi-code /usr/local/bin/kimi
sudo npm uninstall -g @openai/codex
```

The agent stays gone after every resume, fork and deploy from a saved snapshot. The same is true for an apt package that you remove.

If you install your own copy of a tool, your copy is used, not the one that comes with the machine.

## A restore is like a reboot

When a sandbox comes back from a snapshot, it is like a server that restarts.

* Your files, packages and system settings are there.
* **Systemd services that you enabled start again by themselves.**
* **Docker containers that ran start again by themselves.**
* Programs that you started by hand are not running. Start them again, or make them a service.
* Snap packages are reinstalled.

Services and containers start a few seconds after the sandbox is `ready`. Read [Readiness and resume speed](/readiness).

To keep a program running across stops, read [Keep a sandbox running](/long-running-tasks).

## Docker

Docker and BuildKit are installed. This is what a resume, a fork or a deploy from a saved snapshot gets back:

| Docker part | After a resume or fork |
| - | - |
| Named volumes | Saved. All data comes back |
| Containers | boat creates each container again with its settings. Containers that ran start again. A Compose project comes back with `docker compose up` |
| Images that a container uses, from a registry | boat pulls the exact same image again, by digest |
| Images that a container uses, built in the sandbox | Saved in the snapshot, with their tags |
| Other tagged images, also images that no container uses | Saved in the snapshot, with their tags |
| Untagged `<none>` images | Not saved |
| Build cache | Not saved. The first build starts from zero |

A snapshot saves these images at the moment you take it. Do not stop Docker before `boat snapshot`.

After a resume reaches `ready`, images and containers load in the background. They appear about 2 seconds later. Read [Readiness and resume speed](/readiness).

boat pulls the registry images that a container uses from their registry at each resume. A private registry needs its login in the sandbox.

### Docker builds

While a sandbox runs, `docker build` uses its layer cache as usual. A rebuild with no change takes less than one second. The cache is in `/var/lib/docker`, and a snapshot does not save it.

To keep the build cache, save it in your home folder:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
docker buildx build \
  --cache-to type=local,dest=$HOME/.buildcache,mode=max \
  --cache-from type=local,src=$HOME/.buildcache \
  --load -t myapp .
```

We measured this on a Node app with a slow dependency install:

| Build | Time |
| - | - |
| First build, no cache | 38 s |
| Rebuild on the same machine | 0.4 s |
| Rebuild on a fork, with the saved cache | 8 s |

## Tool caches

A snapshot does not save `~/.cache`. Tools that download files into it download them again after a resume or a fork.

Two folders in `~/.cache` are saved:

* `~/.cache/ms-playwright`: the Playwright browsers. `npx playwright install` puts them there by default.
* `~/.cache/deno`: the Deno cache.

To keep the cache of another tool, point that tool at a folder outside `~/.cache`.

## Leave files out with `.boatignore`

Build output and dependency folders slow down every restore, and you can make them again. To leave them out of snapshots, write a `.boatignore` file. The next snapshot uses it.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
cd ~/myapp
printf 'node_modules/\n.next/\n' > .boatignore
```

* It uses the same rules as `.gitignore`.
* Its rules apply to the folder that it is in. A `.boatignore` in a repo applies to that repo. A `.boatignore` in your home folder applies to the whole sandbox.
* boat looks for it up to six folders below your home folder. It does not look inside `node_modules`, `.next`, `target` or `vendor`.
* Put the file at the top of the folder that you want to leave out, not inside it.
* `.git` is always saved, because you cannot make it again.
* boat also reads the old names `.boxignore` and `.oneignore`. If a folder has more than one, `.boatignore` wins.

**boat does not read your `.gitignore`.** A `.gitignore` lists files that you do not commit. That is not the same as files that you can lose. Also, a tool that you install with `git clone` has its own `.gitignore`. For example, the `.gitignore` of `~/.nvm` lists every Node version that you install.


# SSH
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/ssh-access

Open a shell in a sandbox, run commands, forward a port to your computer, connect VS Code or another SSH client, and copy files in and out.

Run `boat ssh <id>` for a shell. The CLI creates the SSH key, authorizes it on the sandbox and checks the host key for you.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat ssh bx_f7k2q9hd
```

In the dashboard, **Copy SSH** in the row menu of a sandbox copies this command.

## Run commands

* For a script or an agent, use `boat exec`. It is faster than `boat ssh` because it opens no SSH session.
* For a long-running server, add `--detach`. A normal command stops after 30 seconds by default. Read [Background commands](/long-running-tasks/background-commands).
* In an integration, use the command API. The examples use `BOAT_API_BASE=https://boat.dev/api/v1`.

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat exec bx_f7k2q9hd --cwd my-repo "npm test"
boat ssh bx_f7k2q9hd "cd /home/user/my-repo && npm test"
boat ssh bx_f7k2q9hd -- bash -s < ./setup.sh
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/bx_f7k2q9hd/commands" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"command":"npm test","cwd":"my-repo","timeoutSeconds":60}'
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
const result = await sandbox.command({
  sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd",
  command: "npm test", cwd: "my-repo", timeoutSeconds: 60,
});
console.log(result.stdout);
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
from boat_sdk.models.command_request import CommandRequest

result = sandbox.command(
    "bx_f7k2q9hd",
    CommandRequest(command="npm test", cwd="my-repo", timeout_seconds=60),
)
print(result.actual_instance.stdout)   # command() returns a wrapper
```

`boat ssh` and `boat exec` without an id use the last sandbox that you created or forked in this terminal. This needs the shell function that the installer adds. In scripts, always pass the id.

> [!NOTE]
>
> * SSH works only while the sandbox runs. Resume a stopped sandbox first.
> * In the first seconds of a start or a resume, SSH can answer `sandbox_restoring` or `sandbox_securing`. Retry a few seconds later. The CLI retries for you.

## Forward a port

Use `boat forward` to reach a port of the sandbox on your own computer. Nothing becomes public. It works for any TCP service, for example a database.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat forward bx_f7k2q9hd --remote 5432                 # sandbox 127.0.0.1:5432 -> your localhost:5432
boat forward bx_f7k2q9hd --remote 3000 --local 8080    # sandbox port 3000 -> your localhost:8080
boat forward bx_f7k2q9hd --reverse --local 7777        # your localhost:7777 -> sandbox 127.0.0.1:7777
```

* The command runs until you press Ctrl+C. It connects again by itself after a network drop.
* `--bind` changes the listen address. The default is `127.0.0.1`.
* The API key needs the `ssh` action.

For a URL that other people can open, read [Public URLs](/hosting).

## Use VS Code, Cursor or another SSH client

The full setup, with an `~/.ssh/config` block, is on [VS Code, Cursor and SSH config](/ssh-access/editors). In short:

1. Authorize your public key on the sandbox.
2. Connect to `sshEndpoint` when it is set. Else connect to `machineIp` on port 22.
3. Pin the host key from the API response.
4. Do steps 1 to 3 again after each resume and fork. The machine, its IP address and its host key change.

The curl tab does all three steps. It uses your own key `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`.

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat ssh bx_f7k2q9hd true   # authorizes ~/.ssh/ascii_box_ed25519 and pins the host key for boat ssh
boat info bx_f7k2q9hd       # "ip", and "sshEndpoint" (host:port) when the sandbox has no public IPv4
ssh -i ~/.ssh/ascii_box_ed25519 user@<ip>                   # when sshEndpoint is null
ssh -i ~/.ssh/ascii_box_ed25519 -p <port> user@<host>       # when sshEndpoint is "host:port"
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
resp="$(curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/bx_f7k2q9hd/sshkey" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"key\":\"$(cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub)\"}")"

echo "bx_f7k2q9hd $(echo "$resp" | jq -r .hostKey)" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts_bx_f7k2q9hd

# sshEndpoint ("host:port") is set when the sandbox has no public IPv4 of its own
endpoint="$(echo "$resp" | jq -r '.sshEndpoint // empty')"
host="${endpoint%:*}"; port="${endpoint##*:}"
[ -n "$endpoint" ] || { host="$(echo "$resp" | jq -r .machineIp)"; port=22; }

ssh -p "$port" -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 \
    -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes \
    -o UserKnownHostsFile=~/.ssh/known_hosts_bx_f7k2q9hd \
    -o HostKeyAlias=bx_f7k2q9hd \
    user@"$host"
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
const { hostKey, machineIp, sshEndpoint } = await sandbox.sshKey({
  sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd",
  key: "ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nza... you@example.com",
});
// write `bx_f7k2q9hd ${hostKey}` to a known_hosts file, then connect with HostKeyAlias=bx_f7k2q9hd
// to sshEndpoint ("host:port") when it is set, else to machineIp on port 22
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
from boat_sdk.models.ssh_key_request import SshKeyRequest

resp = sandbox.ssh_key("bx_f7k2q9hd", SshKeyRequest(key="ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nza... you@example.com"))
# write f"bx_f7k2q9hd {resp.host_key}" to a known_hosts file, then connect with HostKeyAlias=bx_f7k2q9hd
# to resp.ssh_endpoint ("host:port") when it is set, else to resp.machine_ip on port 22
```

* The CLI tab trusts the host key on the first connection. Use the curl tab to pin the key.
* The host key comes over your API connection, not over SSH. You can trust it without a first-connection prompt.
* An authorized key stays in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the sandbox. Stop, resume and fork keep it.
* The CLI key file keeps its old name, `~/.ssh/ascii_box_ed25519`.

### "REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED"

Every resume and every fork runs the sandbox on a new machine with a new host key. `boat ssh` and `boat scp` get the new key for you. For another client, call the SSH key endpoint again and replace the line in your known_hosts file.

## Copy files

* From a terminal, use `boat scp` with the sandbox ID as the remote host. Add `-r` for a folder.
* In an integration, use the file and artifact API calls.

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat scp ./local-file.txt bx_f7k2q9hd:/home/user/
boat scp bx_f7k2q9hd:/home/user/output.zip ./output.zip
boat scp -r ./my-folder bx_f7k2q9hd:/home/user/
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
curl -sS -X PUT "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/bx_f7k2q9hd/files" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"path":"notes/input.txt","content":"hello\n","encoding":"utf8"}'

curl -L -o output.zip "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/bx_f7k2q9hd/artifacts?path=output.zip" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY"
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
await sandbox.writeFile({
  sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd",
  path: "notes/input.txt", content: "hello\n", encoding: "utf8",
});

const artifact = await sandbox.artifact({ sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd", path: "output.zip" });
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
from boat_sdk.models.file_write_request import FileWriteRequest

sandbox.write_file("bx_f7k2q9hd", FileWriteRequest(
    path="notes/input.txt",
    content="hello\n",
    encoding="utf8",
))
artifact = sandbox.artifact("bx_f7k2q9hd", "output.zip")
```

File read and write paths follow these rules:

| Path | Rule |
| - | - |
| Relative | boat resolves it from the sandbox work directory, `/home/user`. |
| Absolute | It must resolve under `/home/user` or `/tmp`. |
| Absolute, outside these roots | boat refuses it with a 400 `invalid_path` error. The error names the allowed roots. |

### Large files

The JSON file calls stop at 5 MiB. For a larger file, ask for a signed URL and send the bytes straight to the sandbox. The sandbox serves the URL itself. So boat sets no size limit, and the transfer needs no Authorization header.

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
# Upload: get a URL, then PUT the raw file to it
url=$(curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/bx_f7k2q9hd/files/upload-url" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"path":"data/dataset.parquet"}' | jq -r .url)
curl -sS -X PUT --data-binary @dataset.parquet "$url"

# Download: get a URL, then GET it
url=$(curl -sS -X POST "$BOAT_API_BASE/sandboxes/bx_f7k2q9hd/files/download-url" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"path":"output/model.bin"}' | jq -r .url)
curl -sS -o model.bin "$url"
```

```ts TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
const up = await sandbox.createUploadUrl({ sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd", path: "data/dataset.parquet" });
await fetch(up.url, { method: "PUT", body: await fs.readFile("dataset.parquet") });

const down = await sandbox.createDownloadUrl({ sandboxId: "bx_f7k2q9hd", path: "output/model.bin" });
const bytes = await (await fetch(down.url)).arrayBuffer();
```

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
import requests
from boat_sdk.models.file_url_request import FileUrlRequest

up = sandbox.create_upload_url("bx_f7k2q9hd", FileUrlRequest(path="data/dataset.parquet"))
with open("dataset.parquet", "rb") as f:
    requests.put(up.url, data=f)

down = sandbox.create_download_url("bx_f7k2q9hd", FileUrlRequest(path="output/model.bin"))
open("model.bin", "wb").write(requests.get(down.url).content)
```

* A URL works for one path and one direction (download or upload).
* It expires after 15 minutes. Pass `ttlSeconds` (up to 3600) to change that.
* An upload creates missing directories. It replaces an existing file only when the upload completes.
* Anyone who has the URL can use it until it expires. Do not log it or share it.
* Getting a download URL needs `file.read`. Getting an upload URL needs `file.write`.

For all `scp` options, read [CLI reference](/cli-reference#boat-scp).

## Related

* [VS Code, Cursor and SSH config](/ssh-access/editors)
* [Public URLs](/hosting)
* [Long-running tasks](/long-running-tasks)
* [Desktop streaming](/desktop-streaming)


# VS Code, Cursor and SSH config
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/ssh-access/editors

Open a sandbox in VS Code Remote-SSH or Cursor with an ~/.ssh/config entry, and refresh the address and host key after each resume.

VS Code Remote-SSH and Cursor use the normal OpenSSH client. They read `~/.ssh/config`. The boat CLI does not write that file. Use the script below to write one entry per sandbox.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Each resume and each fork moves the sandbox to a new machine. The address and the SSH host key change. Run the script again after each resume.

## Before you start

* An API key with the `ssh` action in `BOAT_API_KEY`. Read [API keys](/api-keys).
* An SSH key pair at `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`. Create one with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` if you have none.
* `curl` and `jq`.
* On Windows, run the script in Git Bash. VS Code reads the same `C:\Users\<you>\.ssh\config`.

## 1. Save the script

Save this as `boat-ssh-config.sh`:

```bash boat-ssh-config.sh theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: bash boat-ssh-config.sh <sandbox-id>
# Authorizes ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 on the sandbox and writes ~/.ssh/boat/<id>.conf.
set -euo pipefail
id="$1"
key=~/.ssh/id_ed25519

resp="$(curl -fsS -X POST "https://boat.dev/api/v1/sandboxes/$id/sshkey" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOAT_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"key\":\"$(cat "$key.pub")\"}")"

# sshEndpoint ("host:port") is set when the sandbox has no public IPv4 of its own
endpoint="$(echo "$resp" | jq -r '.sshEndpoint // empty')"
if [ -n "$endpoint" ]; then
  host="${endpoint%:*}"; port="${endpoint##*:}"
else
  host="$(echo "$resp" | jq -r .machineIp)"; port=22
fi

mkdir -p ~/.ssh/boat
echo "$id $(echo "$resp" | jq -r .hostKey)" > ~/.ssh/boat/"$id".known_hosts
cat > ~/.ssh/boat/"$id".conf <<EOF
Host $id
  HostName $host
  Port $port
  User user
  IdentityFile "$key"
  HostKeyAlias $id
  UserKnownHostsFile "$HOME/.ssh/boat/$id.known_hosts"
  StrictHostKeyChecking yes
EOF
echo "Wrote ~/.ssh/boat/$id.conf"
```

## 2. Include the entries in your SSH config

Add this line at the **top** of `~/.ssh/config`, before any `Host` line:

```text ~/.ssh/config theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
Include ~/.ssh/boat/*.conf
```

## 3. Write the entry and connect

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
bash boat-ssh-config.sh bx_f7k2q9hd
ssh bx_f7k2q9hd true    # test: prints nothing and exits 0
```

* **VS Code**: install the Remote - SSH extension. Run **Remote-SSH: Connect to Host...** and pick `bx_f7k2q9hd`.
* **Cursor**: run **Remote-SSH: Connect to Host...** and pick `bx_f7k2q9hd`.
* Other tools that read `~/.ssh/config` work the same way.

Open the folder `/home/user/<your-repo>`.

## After a resume or a fork

1. Run `bash boat-ssh-config.sh <id>` again. It writes the new address and the new host key.
2. Reconnect the editor.

For a fork, use the id of the fork. Each sandbox gets its own entry.

If you skip step 1, SSH stops with `REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED` or cannot connect. Do not delete the key check. Run the script.

## Good to know

* An open editor does not delay auto-stop. To keep the sandbox up for a work day, run `boat extend <id> --hours 8`. Read [Auto-stop](/long-running-tasks/auto-stop).
* The editor installs its server in `/home/user/.vscode-server` or a similar folder. Snapshots keep it, so the next connection after a resume is faster.
* Your key stays authorized after a stop, a resume and a fork. The script authorizes it again anyway. This is safe.
* `boat ssh <id>` needs none of this. It finds the address and the host key itself.

## Related

* [SSH](/ssh-access)
* [Forward a port](/ssh-access#forward-a-port)


# Support
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/support

How to reach the boat team by email or Discord, and what to send so we can help on the first reply.

## Contact

| Channel | Use it for |
| - | - |
| Email [support@ascii.dev](mailto:support@ascii.dev) | Account, billing, refunds, a sandbox that misbehaves, security issues, anything private. |
| [Discord](https://discord.gg/Y3TFTmE89g) | Questions, ideas, and help from the team and other users. |

The support address is on `ascii.dev`, the mail domain of the company behind boat. It is the right address for boat.

You do not need to contact us to use a feature that your plan includes. For example, `xlarge` needs only the \$100 plan or higher. Read [Pricing](/pricing).

## What to send

* The email address of your boat account.
* The sandbox ID, for example `bx_23456789`, if one sandbox is affected.
* The command or API call you ran, and the full error text.
* The `requestId` from the API error, if you have one.
* The time it happened, with your time zone.

Do not send API keys, passwords or secret files. We never ask for them.

## Before you write

* Is the platform down? See [status.ascii.dev](https://status.ascii.dev). Uptime, SOC 2 and data location are on [Compliance and uptime](/compliance).
* A sandbox stopped or does not answer? Read [Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting).
* A `429` or another error code? Read [Limits and errors](/limits).


# Troubleshooting
Source: https://docs.boat.dev/troubleshooting

Why a sandbox stopped by itself, what to do when a sandbox does not answer or is in error, out of memory (exit 137), out-of-disk emails, and what common error messages mean.

Start with `boat info <id>`. It shows the state, the auto-stop time (`archiveAfter`), the reason for a stop or a failure (`error`), and the time of the last snapshot (`snapshotCompletedAt`).

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark-default"}}
boat info bx_f7k2q9hd
```

## Why did my sandbox stop?

Auto-stop is the most common cause. A stop by boat keeps the disk, the same as `boat stop`, unless the table says otherwise.

| Cause | How to check | Data |
| - | - | - |
| **Auto-stop.** The default is 1 hour, counted from the create or the last resume. A running prompt moves the time later | `archiveAfter` in `boat info` is in the past | Kept |
| **Empty wallet for 24 hours.** The included time is used and the wallet is empty. boat sends an email, then stops your sandboxes 24 hours later | `boat wallet`. Email "Your sandboxes will stop soon" | Kept |
| **Plan cancelled with an empty wallet.** The stop comes at once, with no 24-hour wait | `boat billing status` | Kept |
| **Free trial used its 25 hours of compute** | `boat billing status`. New starts fail with `trial_compute_limit_reached` | Kept. Read [Free trial](/free-trial) |
| **Forced stop after 3 days of failed saves.** A stop was refused because its snapshot kept failing | Email "could not be stopped" | Kept up to the last good snapshot. Later writes are lost |
| **Machine stopped answering for 3 days**, with no snapshot newer than the failure | Email about a sandbox that stopped responding | Kept up to the last good snapshot. Later writes are lost |
| **Account closed** | Email that confirms the closing | Kept for 30 days. Read [Close your account](/data-retention/close-account) |

Two settings change what a stop keeps:

| Setting | How to check | Data |
| - | - | - |
| [Zero data retention](/data-retention/zero-data-retention) | `boat data-retention status` | Deleted at the stop. You cannot resume |
| [Snapshots off](/data-retention/snapshots-and-monitoring-off#snapshots-off) | `"snapshots": false` in `boat info` | Erased at the stop. You cannot resume |

To get the sandbox back, run `boat resume <id>`.

> [!WARNING]
>
> boat keeps the disk of a stopped sandbox for at least 14 days. After that, automated retention cleanup can delete it once enabled, whatever caused the stop. The job currently reports candidates without deleting them in production. Read [Keep a stopped sandbox longer than 14 days](/snapshots/stop#keep-a-stopped-sandbox-longer-than-14-days).
